pages.caption: And many a hunting song they sung, And song of game and glee.
Then tuned to plaintive strains their tongue, "Of Scotland's luve and lee."
To wilder measures next they turn "The Black, Black Bull of Norroway!"
Sudden the tapers cease to burn, The minstrels cease to play.
"The Cout of Keeldar," by J. Leyden.
In Norroway, langsyne, there lived a certain lady, and she had three dochters.
The auldest o' them said to her mither: "Mither, bake me a bannock, and roast me a collop, for I'm gaun awa' to seek my fortune."
pages.scene: Eldest daughter asks to seek fortune

pages.caption: Her mither did sae.
And the dochter gaed awa' to an auld witch washerwife and telled her purpose.
The auld wife bade her stay that day, and gang and look out o' her back door, and see what she could see.
She saw nocht the first day.
pages.scene: First day of watching yields nothing

pages.caption: The second day she did the same, and saw nocht.
On the third day she looked again, and saw a coach-and-six coming along the road.
pages.scene: Coach and six arrives for eldest

pages.caption: She ran in and telled the auld wife what she saw.
"Aweel," quo' the auld wife, "yon's for you."
Sae they took her into the coach, and galloped aff.
The second dochter next says to her mither: "Mither, bake me a bannock, and roast me a collop, fur I'm gaun awa' to seek my fortune."
pages.scene: Second daughter asks to seek fortune

pages.caption: Her mither did sae; and awa' she gaed to the auld wife, as her sister had dune.
On the third day she looked out o' the back door, and saw a coach-and-four coming along the road.
pages.scene: Coach and four arrives for second

pages.caption: "Aweel," quo' the auld wife, "yon's for you." Sae they took her in, and aff they set.
The third dochter says to her mither: "Mither, bake me a bannock, and roast me a collop, for I'm gaun awa' to seek my fortune."
pages.scene: Third daughter asks to seek fortune

pages.caption: Her mither did sae; and awa' she gaed to the auld witch-wife.
She bade her look out o' her back door, and see what she could see.
She did sae; and when she came back said she saw nocht.
pages.scene: Third daughter sees nothing first day

pages.caption: The second day she did the same, and saw nocht.
The third day she looked again, and on coming back said to the auld wife she saw nocht but a muckle Black Bull coming roaring alang the road.
pages.scene: The Black Bull appears on the road

pages.caption: "Aweel," quo' the auld wife, "yon's for you."
pages.description: [Old wife declares the bull for her]
pages.scene: Witch declares the bull is hers

pages.caption: On hearing this she was next to distracted wi' grief and terror; but she was lifted up and set on his back, and awa' they went.
pages.scene: Third daughter is lifted onto the bull

pages.caption: Aye they traveled, and on they traveled, till the lady grew faint wi' hunger.
pages.scene: Long journey begins, lady grows hungry

pages.caption: "Eat out o' my right lug," says the Black Bull, "and drink out o' my left lug, and set by your leavings."
pages.scene: Bull offers food and drink from his ears

pages.caption: Sae she did as he said, and was wonderfully refreshed.
pages.scene: Lady is refreshed by the magical food

pages.caption: And lang they gaed, and sair they rade, till they came in sight o' a very big and bonny castle.
pages.scene: Castle comes into view in the distance

pages.caption: "Yonder we maun be this night," quo' the bull; "for my auld brither lives yonder."
pages.scene: Bull explains it is his brother's castle

pages.caption: And presently they were at the place.
They lifted her aff his back, and took her in, and sent him away to a park for the night.
pages.scene: Lady taken inside, bull sent to park

pages.caption: In the morning, when they brought the bull hame, they took the lady into a fine shining parlor.
And gave her a beautiful apple, telling her no to break it till she was in the greatest strait ever mortal was in in the world, and that wad bring her o't.
Again she was lifted on the bull's back.
And after she had ridden far, and farer than I can tell, they came in sight o' a far bonnier castle, and far farther awa' than the last.
Says the bull till her: "Yonder we maun be the night, for my second brither lives yonder."
And they were at the place directly.
They lifted her down and took her in, and sent the bull to the field for the night.
pages.scene: Lady taken in, bull sent to field

pages.caption: In the morning they took the lady into a fine and rich room.
And gave her the finest pear she had ever seen, bidding her no to break it till she was in the greatest strait ever mortal could be in, and that wad get her out o't.
Again she was lifted and set on his back, and awa' they went.
pages.scene: Lady mounts bull for third journey

pages.caption: And lang they gaed, and sair they rade, till they came in sight o' the far biggest castle, and far farthest aff, they had yet seen.
pages.scene: Third and greatest castle comes into view

pages.caption: "We maun be yonder the night," says the bull, "for my young brither lives yonder."
And they were there directly.
They lifted her down, took her in, and sent the bull to the field for the night.
pages.scene: Lady taken in, bull sent to field

pages.caption: In the morning they took her into a room, the finest of a'.
pages.scene: Lady brought to the finest room

pages.caption: And gied her a plum, telling her no to break it till she was in the greatest strait mortal could be in, and that wad get her out o't.
Presently they brought hame the bull, set the lady on his back, and awa' they went.
And aye they gaed, and on they rade, till they came to a dark and ugsome glen, where they stopped, and the lady lighted down.
pages.scene: Arrival at the dark and fearsome glen

pages.caption: Says the bull to her: "Here ye maun stay till I gang and fight the deil."
pages.scene: Bull prepares to fight the devil

pages.caption: Ye maun seat yoursel' on that stane, and move neither hand nor fit till I come back, else I'll never find ye again.
pages.scene: Bull tells lady to sit on stone

pages.caption: And if everything round about ye turns blue I hae beated the deil; but should a' things turn red he'll hae conquered me.
pages.scene: Bull explains the signs of victory

pages.caption: She set hersel' down on the stane, and by-and-by a' round her turned blue.
pages.description: [Lady sits on stone, world turns blue]
pages.scene: World turns blue as bull wins

pages.caption: O'ercome wi' joy, she lifted the ae fit and crossed it owre the ither, sae glad was she that her companion was victorious.
pages.scene: Lady crosses her foot in joy

pages.caption: The bull returned and sought for but never could find her.
pages.scene: Bull returns but she is gone

pages.caption: Lang she sat, and aye she grat, till she wearied.
pages.scene: Lady weeps alone on the stone

pages.caption: At last she rase and gaed awa', she kedna whaur till.
pages.scene: Lady wanders off into the unknown

pages.caption: On she wandered till she came to a great hill o' glass, that she tried a' she could to climb, bat wasna able.
Round the bottom o' the hill she gaed, sabbing and seeking a passage owre, till at last she came to a smith's house.
pages.scene: Lady circles the hill seeking passage

pages.caption: And the smith promised, if she wad serve him seven years, he wad make her iron shoon, wherewi' she could climb owre the glassy hill.
pages.scene: Smith offers iron shoes for seven years

pages.caption: At seven years' end she got her iron shoon.
Clamb the glassy hill, and chanced to come to the auld washerwife's habitation.
There she was telled of a gallant young knight that had given in some bluidy sarks to wash, and whaever washed thae sarks was to be his wife.
pages.scene: Knight seeks wife through washing shirts

pages.caption: The auld wife had washed till she was tired, and then she set to her dochter, and baith washed, and they washed, and they better washed, in hopes of getting the young knight.
pages.description: [Old wife and daughter washing in vain]
pages.scene: Witch and daughter wash but fail

pages.caption: But a' they could do they couldna bring out a stain.
pages.scene: No stain can be removed by them

pages.caption: At length they set the stranger damosel to wark; and whenever she began the stains came out pure and clean.
But the auld wife made the knight believe it was her dochter had washed the sarks.
So the knight and the eldest dochter were to be married, and the stranger damosel was distracted at the thought of it, for she was deeply in love wi' him.
So she bethought her of her apple, and breaking it, found it filled with gold and precious jewelry, the richest she had ever seen.
pages.scene: Apple opens to reveal gold and jewels

pages.caption: "All these," she said to the eldest dochter, "I will give you, on condition that you put off your marriage for ae day, and allow me to go into his room alone at night."
pages.scene: Lady bargains for one night alone

pages.caption: So the lady consented; but meanwhile the auld wife had prepared a sleeping-drink, and given it to the knight, wha drank it, and never wakened till next morning.
The lee-lang night ther damosel sabbed and sang:
"Seven lang years I served for thee, The glassy hill I clamb for thee, The bluidy shirt I wrang for thee; And wilt thou no wauken and turn to me?"
Next day she kentna what to do for grief.
She then brak the pear, and found it filled wi' jewelry far richer than the contents o' the apple.
Wi' thae jewels she bargained for permission to be a second night in the young knight's chamber.
But the auld wife gied him anither sleeping-drink, and he again sleepit till morning.
A' night she kept sighing and singing as before:
But that day when he was out at the hunting, somebody asked him what noise and moaning was yon they heard all last night in his bedchamber.
pages.scene: Hunters ask about the strange noises

pages.caption: He said he heardna ony noise.
But they assured him there was sae; and he resolved to keep waking that night to try what he could hear.
That being the third night, and the damosel being between hope and despair.
She brak her plum, and it held far the richest jewelry of the three.
She bargained as before; and the auld wife, as before, took in the sleeping-drink to the young knight's chamber; but he telled her he couldna drink it that night without sweetening.
pages.scene: Knight pretends to drink the potion

pages.caption: And when she gaed awa' for some honey to sweeten it wi', he poured out the drink, and sae made the auld wife think he had drunk it.
pages.scene: Knight secretly pours out the potion

pages.caption: They a' went to bed again, and the damosel began, as before, singing:
pages.scene: Lady begins singing for the third time

pages.caption: "Seven lang years I served for thee, The glassy hill I clamb for thee, The bluidy shirt I wrang for thee; And wilt thou no wauken and turn to me?"
pages.scene: Song of seven years service repeated

pages.caption: He heard, and turned to her.
And she telled him a' that had befa'en her, and he telled her a' that had happened to him.
And he caused the auld washerwife and her dochter to be burned.
pages.scene: Wicked witch and daughter are burned

pages.caption: And they were married, and he and she are living happy till this day, for aught I ken.
(1) Chambers, Popular Traditions of Scotland.
